lessons.title: Earth's Atmosphere: Past and Present
lessons.description: How the atmosphere formed, why it is now mostly nitrogen and oxygen, and how we know.
lessons.content_html:
The Atmosphere Today

The air around us has a remarkably stable composition. Today’s atmosphere is approximately 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, with about 1% of other gases including argon (roughly 0.9%), carbon dioxide (about 0.04%) and water vapour. This composition has been relatively stable for approximately 200 million years. Yet Earth’s early atmosphere was completely different — understanding how it changed, and what evidence tells us this, is a key part of chemistry’s story about our planet.

Key Fact

The current atmosphere is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and 1% other gases (mainly argon with a small amount of carbon dioxide). This composition has been relatively stable for around 200 million years.

The Early Atmosphere

About 4.6 billion years ago, when Earth first formed, there was no free oxygen in the atmosphere. Scientists believe intense volcanic activity during the first billion years produced a very different atmosphere: mainly carbon dioxide, with some water vapour, nitrogen, methane and ammonia — similar to the current atmospheres of Mars and Venus. As Earth gradually cooled, the water vapour condensed to form the oceans. Some carbon dioxide dissolved in this new ocean water, removing it from the atmosphere.

No direct sample of Earth’s early atmosphere survives, so scientists piece together evidence from multiple sources. Ancient rocks provide clues — the chemical composition of very old rocks shows what gases were available in the environment when they formed. The absence of rust-like oxidised iron minerals in very ancient rocks, for example, suggests there was little or no free oxygen.

Ice cores drilled from Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets preserve trapped air bubbles from up to around 800,000 years ago, allowing scientists to directly measure past atmospheric compositions. Volcanic emissions today still contain carbon dioxide, water vapour and sulfur dioxide, supporting the idea that early volcanoes produced a similar mixture. Comparison with other planets — Mars and Venus both have atmospheres that are mostly carbon dioxide — provides further circumstantial support that Earth’s early atmosphere was similar before photosynthesis changed it.

This is an important example of how science works: where we cannot directly observe or measure the past, we construct explanations from multiple independent sources of evidence. The more independent sources that converge on the same picture, the greater our confidence in the explanation.

How Oxygen Increased

The dramatic increase in atmospheric oxygen is attributed to the evolution of organisms capable of photosynthesis. Early photosynthetic organisms — particularly cyanobacteria — evolved in the oceans around 2.7 billion years ago. They absorbed carbon dioxide and released oxygen as a waste product. Over hundreds of millions of years, this gradually increased the oxygen level in the atmosphere and decreased the carbon dioxide level.

As oxygen levels rose, it accumulated in the upper atmosphere and formed the ozone layer, which absorbs much of the Sun’s harmful ultraviolet radiation. The ozone layer’s formation allowed life to move out of the oceans onto land. Meanwhile, carbon dioxide levels continued to fall as photosynthesis removed it, as some dissolved in the expanding oceans, and as marine organisms used dissolved carbon dioxide to build calcium carbonate shells. Over geological time, these shells became compressed into sedimentary rocks such as limestone, locking carbon away. The organic carbon in dead organisms eventually formed fossil fuels — coal, oil and natural gas.

Key Fact

Carbon dioxide decreased by three routes: dissolving in the oceans; being used by marine organisms to build calcium carbonate shells that became sedimentary rocks (limestone); and organic carbon in dead organisms becoming fossil fuels over millions of years.

Unlike carbon dioxide, nitrogen is relatively unreactive under normal atmospheric conditions. Small amounts were present in the early volcanic atmosphere and also produced by the action of bacteria on nitrogen-containing compounds. Because nitrogen does not participate in photosynthesis or the formation of sedimentary rocks, it was not ‘locked away’ like carbon dioxide. Instead, as oxygen increased and carbon dioxide decreased, nitrogen became the dominant gas by default — its proportion rose simply because the other gases decreased.

The timeline of atmospheric change spans billions of years: heavy volcanic outgassing in the first billion years produced a CO\(_2\)-rich atmosphere; photosynthesis from roughly 2.7 billion years ago gradually increased oxygen and reduced CO\(_2\); the atmosphere has been roughly its current composition for the last 200 million years, though small changes continue as a result of human activities.

Monitoring Atmospheric Change Today

Although the atmosphere has been relatively stable for about 200 million years, its composition is not fixed. Monitoring stations around the world continuously track the concentration of carbon dioxide and other gases. Data from these stations shows that carbon dioxide levels have risen significantly since industrialisation — a direct result of burning fossil fuels that had locked carbon away for millions of years. This modern change is happening far faster than the natural changes driven by photosynthesis and geological processes over billions of years. Understanding the history of the atmosphere — how it formed, how it changed, and why it became stable — gives us the scientific context to evaluate what is happening to it now. The evidence for how the atmosphere evolved is the same kind of evidence that now tells us it is changing again: ice cores, atmospheric measurements, and comparisons across time and place all point to the same conclusion.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions about the early atmosphere, you are very likely to be asked to explain your reasoning from evidence — not just state what the early atmosphere contained. Practise answering: “How do scientists know what the early atmosphere was like?” as a 3-mark explain question. Structure your answer using evidence types (ancient rocks, ice cores, volcanic emissions, planetary comparison) and explain what each piece of evidence tells us. Avoid writing “scientists believe” without explaining the basis for that belief.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The early atmosphere was produced by volcanic activity and consisted mainly of carbon dioxide, with water vapour and little or no oxygen — similar to the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today.
  • Photosynthesis by cyanobacteria gradually increased oxygen and decreased carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide was also locked away in sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels. Nitrogen became dominant because it is unreactive and was not removed by any of these processes.
  • Evidence for the early atmosphere comes from ancient rocks, ice cores, volcanic emissions and comparison with other planets — multiple independent sources that support the same explanation.

lessons.title: Energy Changes in Reactions
lessons.description: Why some reactions release heat and others absorb it, and how to measure energy change.
lessons.content_html:
Energy and Chemical Reactions

Every chemical reaction involves a change in energy. This energy is transferred between the system (the reacting chemicals) and the surroundings. Energy is never created or destroyed during a reaction — it is only transferred. Two categories describe the direction of this transfer, and understanding them is fundamental to chemistry.

Exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings — the surroundings get warmer. Familiar examples include combustion (burning wood or gas), neutralisation reactions (acid + alkali), and the reactions that power hand warmers. Endothermic reactions absorb energy from the surroundings — the surroundings get colder. Examples include thermal decomposition reactions, and the dissolving of certain salts in water. Sports cold packs are a practical application: when activated, an endothermic reaction absorbs heat from the surroundings (including an injured limb), cooling the area.

Key Fact

Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings — temperature of surroundings rises. Endothermic reactions take in energy from the surroundings — temperature of surroundings falls. Both involve transfer, never creation or destruction, of energy.

Measuring Energy Changes

You can determine whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic by measuring the temperature change of the surroundings — typically a solution in a container. If the temperature rises, the reaction is exothermic; if it falls, endothermic. A calorimetry experiment uses a polystyrene cup (a good insulator) to minimise heat loss to the environment, giving a more accurate measurement. You record the starting temperature, the maximum or minimum temperature reached, and calculate the temperature change: ΔT = Tₙₐˣ − TₓₜₐⱿₜ.

A student adds excess magnesium powder to 50 cm3 of dilute hydrochloric acid in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rises from 19°C to 38°C. The equation for calculating the heat energy released is:

$$Q = mc\Delta T$$

where \(Q\) is heat energy (joules), \(m\) is the mass of the solution (grams), \(c\) is the specific heat capacity of the solution (we assume it is the same as water: 4.18 J/g/°C), and \(\Delta T\) is the temperature change (degrees Celsius).

Step 1 — Mass: 50 cm3 of water has a mass of approximately 50 g. Step 2 — Temperature change: \(\Delta T = 38 - 19 = 19\)°C. Step 3 — Calculate Q: \(Q = 50 \times 4.18 \times 19 = 3971\) J = approximately 3.97 kJ. This is exothermic (temperature rose). The polystyrene cup reduces heat loss, making the result more accurate, but some heat will still escape so the true value is slightly higher.

Reaction Profiles

A reaction profile is a diagram that shows the energy content of the reactants and products, and the energy barrier that must be overcome for the reaction to proceed. The vertical axis represents energy; the horizontal axis represents the progress of the reaction (sometimes called the reaction pathway). The diagram is not a time graph — it shows energy levels, not rates.

Every reaction profile includes a peak — the top of the energy barrier. The difference between the reactant energy level and the peak is the activation energy. This is the energy needed to start breaking bonds in the reactants. For an exothermic reaction, the products are at a lower energy level than the reactants; the overall energy change is negative (energy is released). For an endothermic reaction, the products are at a higher energy level than the reactants; the overall energy change is positive (energy is absorbed).

When drawing or annotating a reaction profile, you must label four things: (1) the reactants energy level (the starting plateau); (2) the products energy level (the ending plateau); (3) the activation energy (the arrow from reactant level up to the peak); (4) the overall energy change (the arrow from reactant level to product level). For exothermic reactions, the product level is lower — the overall energy change arrow points downward. For endothermic reactions, the product level is higher — the arrow points upward.

A common mistake is forgetting that the activation energy always starts from the reactant energy level (not from zero), and that the overall energy change is measured from reactants to products (not from zero to products). Catalysts reduce the activation energy — they provide an alternative reaction pathway with a lower energy barrier — so they lower the peak of the profile without changing the energy levels of reactants or products.

Key Fact

Activation energy is the minimum energy needed for particles to react — shown on a reaction profile as the gap from the reactant level to the peak. Exothermic: products lower than reactants. Endothermic: products higher than reactants. A catalyst lowers the activation energy without changing reactant or product energy levels.

Bond Energies (Higher)

At the particle level, energy changes arise from the making and breaking of chemical bonds. Breaking bond energy requires energy — breaking bonds is endothermic (an endothermic step — you must put energy in to pull atoms apart). Making bonds releases energy (an exothermic step — energy is given out when new bonds form). The overall energy change of a reaction depends on the balance between these two processes.

Step 1: Count all the bonds broken in the reactants and add up the energy required to break them (using values given in the question). Step 2: Count all the bonds formed in the products and add up the energy released when they form. Step 3: Calculate the overall energy change:

$$\text{energy change} = \text{energy to break bonds} - \text{energy released making bonds}$$

If the result is negative, the reaction is exothermic (more energy released making bonds than required breaking them). If positive, the reaction is endothermic. For example, for \(H_2 + Cl_2 \rightarrow 2HCl\): energy to break bonds = H–H (436 kJ/mol) + Cl–Cl (242 kJ/mol) = 678 kJ/mol. Energy released making bonds = 2 × H–Cl (431 kJ/mol) = 862 kJ/mol. Energy change = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ/mol. Negative, so exothermic.
lessons.exam_tip_html: A very common error is confusing the direction of the activation energy arrow and the overall energy change arrow on a reaction profile. Practise drawing both an exothermic and an endothermic profile and labelling all four features. For bond energy calculations (Higher), a frequent mistake is calculating the energy change the wrong way round — always write the formula first: energy change = energy to break bonds − energy released making bonds. If your answer is negative, the reaction is exothermic.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings (temperature rises); endothermic reactions absorb energy from the surroundings (temperature falls). Energy is transferred, never created or destroyed.
  • A reaction profile shows the energy levels of reactants and products and the activation energy barrier. Exothermic profiles have products at a lower energy level than reactants; endothermic profiles have products at a higher level.
  • At the particle level: breaking bonds requires energy; making bonds releases energy. The overall energy change is determined by whether more energy is released (making bonds) or absorbed (breaking bonds).

lessons.title: Climate Change: Evidence and Causes
lessons.description: Greenhouse gases, the human carbon footprint, and why scientists are confident climate is changing.
lessons.content_html:
The Greenhouse Effect

The greenhouse effect is a natural and essential process. Without it, the average surface temperature on Earth would be around −18°C rather than the roughly 15°C we experience. Radiation from the Sun arrives as short-wavelength visible and ultraviolet light, which passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth’s surface. The warm surface then emits longer-wavelength infrared radiation back towards space. Greenhouse gases — principally carbon dioxide (\(CO_2\)), methane (\(CH_4\)) and water vapour — absorb some of this outgoing infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions, including back towards the surface. This keeps the Earth significantly warmer than it would otherwise be.

The problem is not the greenhouse effect itself — it is the enhancement of it. Human activities since the industrial revolution have significantly increased the concentrations of key greenhouse gases, intensifying the effect and causing average temperatures to rise. This is the scientific basis of global warming.

Key Fact

The greenhouse effect works because greenhouse gases absorb outgoing infrared radiation and re-emit it, including back towards Earth. Increasing the concentration of these gases enhances this warming effect.

Key Greenhouse Gases and Their Sources

The two most important human-influenced greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide and methane. Burning fossil fuels (coal, oil and natural gas) releases \(CO_2\) that was locked away over millions of years. Deforestation reduces the number of trees absorbing \(CO_2\) through photosynthesis, compounding the problem. Agriculture — particularly livestock farming — releases methane from digestion (enteric fermentation), and rice paddies produce methane from waterlogged soil. Landfill sites generate methane as organic waste decomposes in the absence of oxygen. Together, these human activities are steadily raising atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations.

Methane is present in the atmosphere at much lower concentrations than \(CO_2\), but it is a far more potent greenhouse gas over a shorter timescale. Each molecule of methane traps substantially more heat than a molecule of \(CO_2\). However, methane breaks down in the atmosphere over about a decade, whereas \(CO_2\) persists for centuries. Both gases contribute to warming, but for different reasons and on different timescales. Reducing methane emissions from agriculture and landfill can produce relatively quick effects because of its shorter atmospheric lifetime.

Evidence That Climate Is Changing

Scientists use multiple independent lines of evidence to show that the climate is changing and that human activity is the dominant cause. Evaluating the quality of this evidence — and understanding what it does and does not show — is a key scientific skill.

Ice cores — cylinders of ice drilled from ice sheets in Antarctica and Greenland contain tiny air bubbles that preserve samples of ancient atmosphere. Scientists can measure the \(CO_2\) and methane concentrations in these bubbles and compare them with temperatures reconstructed from the ratio of oxygen isotopes in the ice. This data shows a clear correlation between greenhouse gas concentrations and temperature over hundreds of thousands of years, and that current \(CO_2\) levels are higher than at any point in the record. This is strong evidence because ice cores provide a continuous, directly measured record extending far back into Earth’s past.

Temperature records — systematic measurement of global average surface temperatures by weather stations and ocean buoys shows a clear warming trend over the past century and a half. Sea level measurements show that sea levels are rising, consistent with predictions from warming (melting ice and thermal expansion of warmer ocean water). Satellite data confirms that Arctic sea ice extent is declining and glaciers worldwide are retreating. Each of these datasets comes from independent measurement systems, so the fact they all point in the same direction strengthens the overall conclusion.

Key Fact

Ice core data is particularly powerful evidence because it directly measures past greenhouse gas concentrations alongside a temperature proxy, over hundreds of thousands of years. Multiple independent data sources — all pointing to warming — create a robust scientific case.

How Scientific Consensus Forms: Models, Peer Review and Uncertainty

Understanding how scientists became confident about climate change is as important as knowing the facts. Science does not work through a single experiment producing a definitive answer. Instead, it builds through a process of forming hypotheses, gathering data, and revising models in the light of new evidence — a process checked at every stage by peer review.

Climate scientists build complex mathematical models of how the atmosphere and oceans behave. These models are tested against historical climate data: if a model accurately reproduces past climate when given historical inputs, it gives scientists greater confidence that it can predict future trends. No model is perfect — all involve simplifications and assumptions — but when many independent modelling teams around the world produce similar predictions, the agreement itself is a significant finding. Critically, when natural factors alone (such as solar variation and volcanic eruptions) are fed into the models, they cannot reproduce the observed warming pattern. Only when human greenhouse gas emissions are included do the models match the data. This is strong evidence that human activity is the primary driver.

Uncertainty in climate science is not a reason to dismiss its conclusions — it is a reason to understand them precisely. Scientists are very confident that temperatures are rising and that human greenhouse gas emissions are the dominant cause. They are less certain about the exact magnitude of warming over the next century, the regional distribution of effects, and the timing of certain tipping points. These uncertainties arise from the complexity of climate systems (feedbacks between ice cover, ocean currents, water vapour and vegetation), not from doubt about the fundamental mechanism. Acknowledging uncertainty honestly is a sign of rigorous science, not a weakness. This distinction — between what is well-established and what remains uncertain — is a core scientific reasoning skill.

Correlation, Causation and Scientific Reasoning

Climate data shows a clear correlation between rising \(CO_2\) concentrations and rising global temperatures. A common mistake is to assume that correlation automatically proves causation. Here, however, there is not just a correlation — there is also a well-understood physical mechanism (the enhanced greenhouse effect) that explains why more \(CO_2\) leads to more warming. The combination of a strong correlation, a plausible mechanism, and multiple independent lines of supporting evidence is what makes scientists confident that the relationship is causal, not coincidental. When evaluating data about climate change, always ask: is there a mechanism? Do independent sources of evidence agree?

Key Fact

Correlation between rising \(CO_2\) and rising temperatures is supported by a clear physical mechanism (enhanced greenhouse effect) and multiple independent datasets. This combination — correlation plus mechanism plus converging evidence — justifies the scientific conclusion that human emissions are causing warming.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When asked to ‘evaluate the evidence’ for climate change, do not simply list evidence. Show your reasoning: identify the strength of each piece (e.g. ice cores provide a long direct record), acknowledge limitations or uncertainties (models are simplified; natural variation exists), and reach a conclusion. The command word ‘suggest’ may ask you to apply climate science to a novel context — focus on the mechanism rather than memorised facts. In extended responses, balance scientific evidence against uncertainty without overstating either side.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The greenhouse effect is a natural and necessary process; problems arise when human activities increase greenhouse gas concentrations, enhancing warming.
  • Multiple independent lines of evidence — ice cores, temperature records, sea level data, satellite observations — all consistently point to human-caused climate change.
  • Scientific confidence comes from the combination of correlation, a clear physical mechanism, peer-reviewed modelling, and converging independent datasets — not from any single experiment.

lessons.title: Potable Water and Treating Pollution
lessons.description: Sources of clean water, treatment processes, and how chemistry helps supply communities safely.
lessons.content_html:
Why Water Treatment Matters

Access to safe water is one of the most fundamental public health challenges in the world. In the UK, water from rivers, lakes and reservoirs contains dissolved minerals, suspended solids and potentially harmful microorganisms. It must be processed before it is safe to drink. In many parts of the world — particularly arid regions and areas affected by drought or contamination — obtaining even basic safe water is a daily challenge that chemistry helps address. This lesson covers how potable water is produced from fresh water sources, how seawater is treated in water-scarce regions, and how pollution from human activity is managed.

What ‘Potable’ Means

Potable water is not the same as pure water in the chemical sense. Pure water contains only \(H_2O\) molecules. Potable water still contains dissolved mineral salts and trace amounts of other substances — but at concentrations low enough that it is safe for human consumption. Standards for potable water specify maximum concentrations of dissolved substances, levels of microorganisms, and other quality parameters. In the UK, these standards are set and enforced by regulators, and tap water routinely meets them.

Key Fact

Potable water is safe to drink but is not chemically pure — it still contains dissolved minerals. Pure water contains only \(H_2O\). The key measure for potability is that harmful substances are below safe thresholds.

Producing Potable Water from Fresh Water

In the UK and most countries with reliable fresh water sources, potable water is produced from rivers, lakes and reservoirs through a two-stage treatment process: filtration followed by sterilisation.

Step 1 — Filtration: Water is passed through beds of sand and gravel. The physical structure of these beds traps suspended particles — silt, organic debris and some microorganisms — leaving the water visually clear. This is a physical process, not a chemical one, and it does not remove dissolved substances or microorganisms that have passed through.

Step 2 — Sterilisation: Chlorine is most commonly added to kill remaining bacteria and other harmful microorganisms. Chlorine is favoured because it is effective, relatively inexpensive, and — crucially — it continues to protect water against microbial regrowth as it travels through the distribution network to homes and businesses. Alternatively, ozone (\(O_3\)) or ultraviolet (UV) light can be used; both kill microorganisms effectively but do not provide the lasting protection in the pipes that chlorine does.

Desalination: Water for Arid Regions

In countries or regions where fresh water is scarce — such as parts of the Middle East, North Africa and island communities — seawater or brackish water must be processed to make it potable. This is called desalination. Two methods are used:

Distillation: Seawater is boiled and the steam is collected and condensed. Because the dissolved salts remain in the boiling vessel, the condensed water is essentially pure. This method is energy-intensive, which makes it expensive, but it produces very pure water and is well understood.

Reverse osmosis: Water is forced at high pressure through a semi-permeable membrane with very small pores that block the dissolved salt ions but allow water molecules to pass through. This approach is more energy-efficient than distillation but the membranes require careful maintenance and can become fouled with impurities. Reverse osmosis is increasingly used in large-scale desalination plants because its energy cost is lower and the technology has improved considerably.

Both methods produce concentrated brine (salt water) as a by-product that must be disposed of carefully to avoid environmental damage to marine ecosystems near the outfall. In the UK, where rainfall is generally plentiful, desalination is rarely needed and fresh-water treatment is far more cost-effective. The choice of method is always a balance of economic cost, energy availability and environmental impact.

Key Fact

Desalination (by distillation or reverse osmosis) removes dissolved salts from seawater to make it potable. Both methods require significant energy, making desalination expensive — it is used where fresh water is scarce and no cheaper alternative exists.

Treating Waste Water and Controlling Pollution

Human activity produces large volumes of waste water from homes, industry and agriculture. This water cannot be returned to rivers or seas untreated without causing serious harm to aquatic ecosystems and human health. Waste water treatment is a multi-stage process involving physical and biological steps:

In sewage treatment, waste water is first screened to remove large solids. It then passes into settlement tanks where smaller solid particles sink as sludge. The remaining liquid undergoes biological treatment in which aerobic bacteria break down dissolved organic compounds. The cleaned water (effluent) is filtered and sterilised before being returned to rivers. The sludge removed at earlier stages is treated separately — it may be digested by bacteria (anaerobic digestion, which also produces methane as a useful biogas), dried, and in some cases used as agricultural fertiliser.

Industrial waste water may contain dissolved heavy metals, toxic organic compounds or acids that cannot be removed by standard biological treatment. These require specialist chemical treatment — for example, precipitation reactions to remove dissolved metals, or activated carbon filtration to adsorb organic pollutants. Agricultural run-off containing excess fertilisers is another serious problem. When nitrates and phosphates enter waterways, they cause eutrophication: algae grow rapidly on the excess nutrients, block sunlight from aquatic plants, then die and decompose. The decomposition uses up dissolved oxygen, suffocating fish and other aquatic life. Controlling fertiliser use and managing run-off from fields is therefore important not just for farming economics but for ecosystem health.

Key Fact

In waste water treatment, physical screening and sedimentation remove solids; biological treatment by aerobic bacteria removes dissolved organics. Untreated agricultural run-off can cause eutrophication, depleting oxygen and killing aquatic life.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When describing water treatment, use process order: filtration first (physical, removes solids), then sterilisation (kills microorganisms). A very common error is to name the steps in the wrong order or to confuse filtration with sterilisation. In ‘suggest’ questions about water supply in an unfamiliar context (e.g. a remote island), apply the principles: is fresh water available? If not, desalination is needed; which method is more practical given energy supply? Show you are applying the science, not just listing facts.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Potable water is safe to drink but not chemically pure; it is produced from fresh water by filtration (removes solids) then sterilisation (kills microorganisms, usually with chlorine).
  • Where fresh water is scarce, desalination by distillation or reverse osmosis converts seawater to potable water, but both methods are energy-intensive and expensive.
  • Waste water is treated by screening, sedimentation and biological breakdown before return to waterways; agricultural fertiliser run-off causes eutrophication if not controlled.

lessons.title: Atomic Structure and Models Through Time
lessons.description: Sub-atomic particles, isotopes, and how the atomic model evolved from Dalton to Bohr.
lessons.content_html:
The Structure of the Atom

An atom is the smallest particle of an element that retains the chemical properties of that element. Atoms are extraordinarily small — a typical atomic radius is around \(1 \times 10^{-10}\) m. At the centre of each atom is a tiny, dense nucleus. The nucleus contains two types of subatomic particle: protons, which carry a positive charge, and neutrons, which carry no charge. Electrons orbit the nucleus in energy levels (also called shells) and carry a negative charge. The nucleus accounts for almost all of the mass of an atom, yet it occupies only a tiny fraction of the atom’s volume — the rest is essentially empty space.

Key Fact

Subatomic particles: Proton — charge +1, relative mass 1. Neutron — charge 0, relative mass 1. Electron — charge −1, relative mass approximately \(\frac{1}{1836}\) (negligible). The nuclear radius is far smaller than the atomic radius — most of an atom is empty space.

Atomic Number, Mass Number and Neutrons

The atomic number (also called the proton number) tells you how many protons are in the nucleus. It uniquely identifies the element — all atoms of the same element have the same atomic number. In a neutral atom, the number of protons equals the number of electrons, so the atom has no overall charge. The mass number is the total count of protons plus neutrons in the nucleus. To find the number of neutrons:

$$\text{neutrons} = \text{mass number} - \text{atomic number}$$

For example, a chlorine atom with mass number 35 and atomic number 17 has \(35 - 17 = 18\) neutrons, 17 protons, and 17 electrons. Standard notation places the mass number top-left and the atomic number bottom-left of the symbol: \(^{35}_{17}\text{Cl}\).

Isotopes

Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. Because the number of protons (and therefore electrons) is unchanged, isotopes have identical chemical properties. Only their mass differs. For example, carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons, while carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons. Both are carbon; both react in the same way chemically. Chlorine exists in nature as two isotopes — chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 — which is why the relative atomic mass of chlorine given in the periodic table is approximately 35.5 (a weighted average of the two). Isotopes are important in applications ranging from medical imaging to carbon dating.

An ion is an atom (or group of atoms) that has gained or lost electrons and therefore carries an overall electric charge. Losing electrons produces a positive ion (cation) because there are now more protons than electrons. Gaining electrons produces a negative ion (anion). The nucleus does not change when an ion forms — only the electron count changes. For example, sodium loses one electron to form \(\text{Na}^+\) and chlorine gains one electron to form \(\text{Cl}^-\). The charges are shown as superscripts: \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) has lost two electrons; \(\text{O}^{2-}\) has gained two.

How the Atomic Model Developed

Our current understanding of the atom was not established in a single discovery. It developed gradually over more than a century as new experimental evidence challenged existing ideas and forced scientists to revise their models. This process illustrates a key principle of science: a model is only useful as long as it fits the available evidence. When new evidence arrives that a model cannot explain, the model must change. This is not a failure — it is how science makes progress.

Early 1800s

Dalton’s Model

John Dalton proposed that atoms were tiny, solid, indivisible spheres. He argued that all atoms of the same element were identical and that atoms of different elements had different masses. This model explained why elements always combine in fixed ratios, but gave no internal structure for the atom.

1897

Thomson’s Plum Pudding Model

J.J. Thomson discovered the electron by experimenting with cathode rays. He realised atoms contained smaller, negatively charged particles and proposed a new model: a ball of diffuse positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it — like plums in a pudding. This was the first model to include subatomic particles.

1909–1911

Rutherford’s Nuclear Model

Ernest Rutherford, working with Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, fired positively charged alpha particles at a thin gold foil. The result was unexpected: most particles passed straight through, but some were deflected at large angles and a small number bounced almost directly back. The plum pudding model predicted that alpha particles would pass through the diffuse positive charge with only minor deflections. The actual results could only be explained if the positive charge and most of the mass were concentrated in a tiny, dense region — the nucleus. Rutherford’s nuclear model replaced the plum pudding model.

1913

Bohr’s Model

Niels Bohr refined the nuclear model by showing that electrons could not orbit at any distance — they were confined to specific energy levels (fixed shells) at set distances from the nucleus. Electrons in a given shell have a fixed energy; they can absorb energy and jump to a higher shell, or fall back and release energy as light. Bohr’s model explained the emission spectra of elements, which the Rutherford model could not.

Key Fact

The alpha particle scattering experiment showed that most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil (atom is mostly empty space) but some bounced back sharply (small, dense, positive nucleus). This disproved Thomson’s plum pudding model and led to the nuclear model.

Models as Tools: Strengths and Limitations

Each atomic model was the best explanation of the evidence available at the time. Dalton’s model was useful for explaining chemical reactions but could not account for electrical phenomena. Thomson’s model incorporated electrons but placed them in the wrong configuration. Rutherford’s model identified the nucleus but could not explain why electrons did not spiral into it. Bohr’s model resolved this by proposing fixed energy levels. Later developments in quantum mechanics produced an even more sophisticated picture — but at GCSE, the Bohr model is the accepted working model. Understanding that models change with evidence is as important as knowing the models themselves.

Electronic Configuration

Electrons occupy shells around the nucleus. The first shell holds a maximum of 2 electrons; the second and third shells each hold a maximum of 8. Electrons always fill the lowest available shell first. The electronic configuration of an element determines how it reacts chemically.

Use the atomic number to find the total number of electrons in a neutral atom. Fill shells in order: first shell up to 2, then second up to 8, then third up to 8. Examples: sodium (atomic number 11) → 2, 8, 1. Calcium (atomic number 20) → 2, 8, 8, 2. The number of electrons in the outer shell equals the group number for Groups 1–7. This is why elements in the same group have similar chemical behaviour: they have the same number of outer-shell electrons available for bonding.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about the development of atomic models, name the scientist, describe the evidence or experiment, and explain what it showed that previous models could not explain. Simply naming a model without the experimental evidence behind it will not score full marks. For isotopes, be precise: same element (same proton number), different mass number (different neutron number), same chemical properties. The words ‘same’ and ‘different’ must appear in your answer to score well on comparison questions.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Atoms consist of a nucleus (protons + neutrons) surrounded by electrons in shells; protons are positive, neutrons are neutral, electrons are negative with negligible mass.
  • Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different mass numbers (different neutron counts); they have identical chemical properties.
  • Atomic models evolved from Dalton (solid sphere) → Thomson (plum pudding) → Rutherford (nuclear, from gold-foil experiment) → Bohr (fixed electron shells), each driven by new experimental evidence.

lessons.title: Periodic Table and Chemical Patterns
lessons.description: Group 1, Group 7, Group 0 trends and how electron arrangement explains reactivity.
lessons.content_html:
The Periodic Table: Order from Evidence

The periodic table is one of the most powerful tools in chemistry because it predicts properties before a substance is even made. Elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number (the number of protons), and the arrangement reveals deep patterns in reactivity, bonding, and physical properties. Elements in the same vertical column — a group — share the same number of outer-shell electrons and behave chemically in similar ways. Elements in the same horizontal row — a period — have the same number of electron shells.

Dmitri Mendeleev (1834–1907) published an early version of the periodic table in 1869, arranging elements primarily by atomic mass and grouping them by similar properties. Where the pattern demanded it, he left gaps — predicting the existence and properties of undiscovered elements. When these elements were later discovered (such as gallium in 1875 and germanium in 1886), their properties closely matched Mendeleev’s predictions. This was powerful evidence that the periodic pattern was real, not coincidental. The later shift to ordering by atomic number resolved anomalies where ordering by mass alone would have placed elements in the wrong group (e.g. iodine and tellurium). Mendeleev’s willingness to leave gaps and make falsifiable predictions is a model of good scientific reasoning.

Group 1: The Alkali Metals

Group 1 elements — lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium and francium — are known as the alkali metals. They each have one electron in their outer shell. This single electron is lost easily during reactions, making them highly reactive. All form +1 ions and dissolve in water to produce alkaline solutions (hence their name). They are soft metals: lithium, sodium and potassium can all be cut with a knife. Their low density means lithium, sodium and potassium float on water.

When alkali metals react with water, they produce a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas. The general equation is: \(2M(s) + 2H_2O(l) \rightarrow 2MOH(aq) + H_2(g)\). The reaction becomes more vigorous going down the group: lithium fizzes gently, sodium melts into a ball and fizzes energetically, potassium ignites and burns with a lilac flame. Reactivity increases down Group 1 because the outer electron is further from the nucleus, experiences greater shielding from inner electrons, and is therefore more easily lost.

Key Fact

Group 1 metals have one outer-shell electron. Reactivity increases going down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner shells, making it easier to lose. Melting points decrease going down the group.

Group 7: The Halogens

Group 7 elements — fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine — are called the halogens. They each have seven electrons in their outer shell and need to gain one more electron to achieve a full outer shell, forming −1 ions. Halogens exist as diatomic molecules (\(F_2\), \(Cl_2\), \(Br_2\), \(I_2\)). Physical properties change systematically down the group: fluorine is a pale yellow gas, chlorine is a green gas, bromine is a red-brown liquid at room temperature, and iodine is a dark grey solid that produces a purple vapour when warmed. Melting and boiling points increase going down the group as molecules become larger and intermolecular forces grow stronger.

Reactivity decreases going down Group 7 because the outer shell is further from the nucleus and more shielded. This means the attraction for an incoming electron is weaker, so it becomes harder to gain the additional electron needed to reach a full outer shell.

A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halogen from a solution of its salt. For example, chlorine displaces bromine from potassium bromide solution because chlorine is more reactive than bromine: \(Cl_2(aq) + 2KBr(aq) \rightarrow 2KCl(aq) + Br_2(aq)\). The solution turns from colourless to orange-brown as bromine is released. Bromine can similarly displace iodine from potassium iodide solution. However, bromine cannot displace chlorine from potassium chloride because bromine is less reactive than chlorine. These displacement reactions provide direct experimental evidence for the reactivity trend in Group 7.

Key Fact

Group 7 reactivity decreases going down the group because the outer shell is further from the nucleus, making it harder to attract and gain the additional electron. Boiling points increase going down as molecules get larger and intermolecular forces increase.

Group 0: The Noble Gases

Group 0 elements — helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon — are called the noble gases. They have full outer electron shells, which gives them great stability. They have no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons, so they exist as individual atoms (monatomic) and do not readily form compounds. Boiling points increase going down the group as atoms become larger and the weak intermolecular forces between them become stronger.

Noble gases have useful applications precisely because of their unreactivity: helium is used in balloons and airships (low density, non-flammable); neon is used in advertising signs (produces a distinctive red-orange glow when electricity passes through it); argon is used in light bulbs and in welding to create an inert atmosphere that prevents oxidation of the hot metal or filament.

Electronic Structure Explains All Group Trends

The patterns across Groups 1, 7 and 0 all share the same root explanation: electronic configuration. Going down any group, atoms have more electron shells. In Group 1, the single outer electron is progressively further from the nucleus and more shielded — it is easier to remove, so reactivity increases. In Group 7, the outer shell’s pull on an incoming electron is progressively weaker — gaining an electron becomes harder, so reactivity decreases. In Group 0, the full outer shell provides stability at every period — all noble gases are unreactive for the same reason. Knowing the electronic configuration of an atom tells you which group it belongs to and predicts how it will behave chemically, even for elements you have never studied before.

An unknown element has electronic configuration 2, 8, 7. You can deduce: it has 3 electron shells (period 3), 7 outer-shell electrons (Group 7), so it is a halogen. It will: exist as a diatomic molecule, form −1 ions, be less reactive than chlorine (which has configuration 2, 8, 7 at period 3 — wait, that IS chlorine: 17 electrons). For a period-4 halogen (e.g. bromine, 2, 8, 18, 7), it would be less reactive than chlorine for the reason above. This kind of reasoning from structure to properties is the core skill the periodic table tests — you are expected to apply it to unfamiliar elements in novel contexts.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When explaining reactivity trends, always give the reason in terms of electron structure — simply stating ‘the outer electron is further away’ is not enough without explaining that this makes it easier to lose (Group 1) or harder to gain (Group 7). In displacement questions, always state which halogen is more reactive and why, then predict whether displacement occurs. ‘Suggest’ questions may give you an unfamiliar Group 1 or Group 7 element and ask you to apply the trend — treat it the same way, just check its position in the group relative to elements you know.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Elements in the same group share the same number of outer-shell electrons, giving them similar chemical properties; reactivity trends within groups are explained by how easily electrons are gained or lost as you move down.
  • Group 1 (alkali metals) — reactivity increases down the group (easier to lose the outer electron); Group 7 (halogens) — reactivity decreases down the group (harder to gain an electron); Group 0 (noble gases) — unreactive due to full outer shells.
  • Mendeleev’s decision to leave gaps and predict undiscovered elements, later confirmed by experiment, demonstrates how scientific models earn confidence through verifiable predictions.

lessons.title: Bonding: Ionic, Covalent and Metallic
lessons.description: How atoms combine, what determines bond type, and how to draw and describe each.
lessons.content_html:
Why Atoms Form Bonds

Atoms are most stable when they have a full outer shell of electrons. Most atoms do not naturally achieve this on their own, so they combine with other atoms through chemical bonding. All chemical bonds involve electrostatic forces — attractions between positive and negative charges. The type of bond that forms depends on whether the atoms are metals or non-metals and on how many outer-shell electrons they have. There are three main types: ionic bonding, covalent bonding and metallic bonding.

Ionic Bonding

Ionic bonding forms between a metal and a non-metal. The metal atom transfers one or more electrons to the non-metal atom. The metal becomes a positively charged ion (cation) because it now has more protons than electrons. The non-metal becomes a negatively charged ion (anion) for the opposite reason. The resulting opposite charges attract each other strongly: this electrostatic force of attraction is the ionic bond.

In sodium chloride (NaCl): sodium (2, 8, 1) loses one electron to become \(\text{Na}^+\) (2, 8), and chlorine (2, 8, 7) gains that electron to become \(\text{Cl}^-\) (2, 8, 8). Both ions now have full outer shells. In magnesium oxide (MgO): magnesium (2, 8, 2) loses two electrons to form \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\), and oxygen (2, 6) gains two to form \(\text{O}^{2-}\). In any ionic compound, billions of ions pack together in a regular three-dimensional arrangement called a giant ionic lattice, where every ion is surrounded by oppositely charged neighbours in all directions.

Key Fact

In ionic bonding, electrons are transferred from metal to non-metal. Both ions achieve full outer shells. Ionic compounds form giant lattices held together by strong electrostatic attraction between opposite charges.

Covalent Bonding

Covalent bonding forms between non-metal atoms. Instead of transferring electrons, the atoms share pairs of electrons. Each shared pair counts as one covalent bond. By sharing, each atom achieves a full outer shell without losing or gaining electrons overall. A single shared pair is a single bond. Two shared pairs form a double bond (e.g. \(O_2\), \(CO_2\)). Three shared pairs form a triple bond (e.g. \(N_2\)).

In water (\(H_2O\)): the oxygen atom shares one pair of electrons with each of two hydrogen atoms, forming two single covalent bonds. In chlorine gas (\(Cl_2\)): two chlorine atoms share one pair of electrons. In carbon dioxide (\(CO_2\)): each oxygen forms a double bond with the central carbon atom. Covalent compounds include simple small molecules (like \(H_2O\), \(CO_2\), \(CH_4\)) and very large networks called giant covalent structures (like diamond and silicon dioxide).

Dot-and-cross diagrams are the standard way to represent electron arrangement in bonds. For covalent bonds, use dots for electrons from one atom and crosses for electrons from the other; draw the outer shells overlapping and place the shared pairs in the overlap. For ionic bonds, show the electron being transferred and enclose each ion in square brackets with its charge written outside. These diagrams are models — they show electron positions but not the three-dimensional shape, bond angles, or relative atomic sizes. Different models (ball-and-stick, space-filling) address these limitations but introduce others. No single model captures everything about a bond; choosing the right one depends on what you need to show.

Key Fact

In covalent bonding, non-metal atoms share electron pairs. Each shared pair is one bond. Both atoms count the shared electrons as their own, giving both a full outer shell.

Metallic Bonding

In a metal, atoms are arranged in a regular lattice structure. The outer-shell electrons are not bound to any individual atom — they are delocalised and free to move throughout the entire metallic structure. This creates a “sea” of mobile electrons surrounding a lattice of positive metal ions. The strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the negative delocalised electrons holds the structure together. This is metallic bonding.

The delocalised electrons explain many properties of metals: they conduct electricity because electrons can move freely to carry charge; they conduct heat well because electrons can transfer energy; metals are malleable and ductile because the positive ions can slide past each other without breaking the bonds with the electron sea. The more delocalised electrons per atom (e.g. aluminium gives three, copper gives one), the stronger the metallic bonding and the higher the melting point.

Comparing Bond Types and Structures

The type of bond present in a substance determines its structure, which in turn determines its bulk properties. Understanding this link is essential:

Giant ionic lattice (e.g. NaCl, MgO) — high melting and boiling points because a large amount of energy is needed to overcome the many strong electrostatic attractions throughout the lattice. Conducts electricity when molten or dissolved in water (ions are free to move) but not when solid (ions are fixed in position).

Simple molecular structure (e.g. \(H_2O\), \(CO_2\), \(CH_4\)) — low melting and boiling points because the weak intermolecular forces between molecules require little energy to overcome. The covalent bonds within each molecule are strong, but they are not broken on melting. Does not conduct electricity (no free ions or electrons). The stronger the intermolecular forces (larger molecules), the higher the boiling point.

Giant covalent structure (e.g. diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide) — very high melting and boiling points because melting requires breaking many strong covalent bonds throughout the whole structure. Diamond does not conduct electricity (all electrons are used in bonding); graphite does conduct electricity because it has one delocalised electron per carbon atom.

Metallic structure — high melting and boiling points (especially for metals with more delocalised electrons per atom). Excellent electrical and thermal conductors due to delocalised electrons. Malleable and ductile because ions can slide.

The periodic table gives you the starting information. Metals on the left — metallic bonding. Non-metals on the right — covalent bonding between non-metals, ionic bonding when a metal and non-metal combine. Group 0 elements do not bond. From bond type, you can predict structure; from structure, you can predict properties. This logical chain — position in table → electron arrangement → bond type → structure → properties — is the engine of chemical prediction.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When asked to explain a property (e.g. ‘why does magnesium oxide have a high melting point?’), always state the bond type, then the structural consequence (giant ionic lattice), then the reason the property follows (many strong electrostatic attractions must be overcome). Three-step explanation. For dot-and-cross diagrams, use square brackets and show charges for ionic compounds. Do not forget to show lone pairs as well as bonding pairs in covalent diagrams — the outer shell must be complete on each atom.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ionic bonding involves electron transfer from metal to non-metal, forming a giant ionic lattice; covalent bonding involves electron sharing between non-metals; metallic bonding involves a lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.
  • Bond type determines structure (giant lattice, simple molecular, metallic) which determines properties (melting point, electrical conductivity, malleability).
  • Dot-and-cross diagrams model how electrons are arranged in bonds; they are useful but limited models that show electron positions but not three-dimensional shape.

lessons.title: Chemical Equations and Conservation of Mass
lessons.description: Writing balanced equations, state symbols and explaining what happens at the particle level.
lessons.content_html:
Chemical Formulae: Reading the Language of Chemistry

Chemical formulae represent substances using element symbols and subscript numbers. The subscript number applies to the element immediately before it: \(H_2O\) contains 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom; \(CaCO_3\) contains 1 calcium, 1 carbon and 3 oxygen atoms; \(CO_2\) contains 1 carbon and 2 oxygen atoms. A coefficient (a large number written in front of a formula) multiplies every atom in that formula: \(2H_2O\) means two water molecules, so 4 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms in total. Working out formulae from names requires knowing the charges of common ions: \(Na^+\) and \(Cl^-\) combine in a 1:1 ratio to give NaCl; \(Mg^{2+}\) and \(O^{2-}\) combine in a 1:1 ratio to give MgO; \(Al^{3+}\) and \(O^{2-}\) must combine in a 2:3 ratio to give \(Al_2O_3\).

Writing Chemical Equations

A chemical equation shows what happens in a chemical reaction: reactants on the left of the arrow (\(\rightarrow\)) and products on the right. A word equation uses the names of substances: magnesium + oxygen \(\rightarrow\) magnesium oxide. A symbol equation uses formulae: \(2Mg + O_2 \rightarrow 2MgO\). Symbol equations carry more information — they show the ratio of atoms reacting — and must be balanced.

Conservation of Mass and Balancing Equations

The conservation of mass is a fundamental principle: in a chemical reaction, atoms are rearranged but never created or destroyed. Therefore, the number of each type of atom must be the same on both sides of the equation. Balancing involves adding coefficients (never changing subscript numbers in formulae) until both sides match.

Balance the combustion of methane: \(CH_4 + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + H_2O\)

Step 1 — Count atoms on each side: Left: 1 C, 4 H, 2 O. Right: 1 C, 2 H, 2 O. Carbon is balanced. Hydrogen is not (4 vs 2). Oxygen may need revisiting.

Step 2 — Balance hydrogen: Put a 2 in front of \(H_2O\): \(CH_4 + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O\). Now: Left: 1 C, 4 H, 2 O. Right: 1 C, 4 H, 4 O. Oxygen is now unbalanced (2 vs 4).

Step 3 — Balance oxygen: Put a 2 in front of \(O_2\): \(CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O\). Now: Left: 1 C, 4 H, 4 O. Right: 1 C, 4 H, 4 O. Balanced.

Check: count every atom type on both sides. The equation is correct when every count matches. Never change the subscript numbers — that would change the substance itself.

Key Fact

Equations must be balanced because mass is conserved — atoms are not created or destroyed. To balance: count atoms on each side, add coefficients in front of formulae until both sides match, and never change the subscript numbers in a formula.

State Symbols

State symbols provide additional information about the physical form of each substance at the conditions of the reaction. They are written in brackets after each formula:

  • (s) — solid
  • (l) — liquid
  • (g) — gas
  • (aq) — aqueous (dissolved in water)

For example, the reaction of sodium with water: \(2Na(s) + 2H_2O(l) \rightarrow 2NaOH(aq) + H_2(g)\). State symbols help you understand reaction conditions: an (aq) label tells you the substance is in solution; (g) tells you a gas is released.

Conservation of Mass: Experimental Evidence

Conservation of mass can be verified experimentally. If a reaction is carried out in a sealed container and the total mass is measured before and after, it remains the same. However, in reactions carried out in open containers, the mass may appear to change: if a gas is produced and escapes, the total mass of the remaining substances decreases; if a substance from the air (such as oxygen) is incorporated, the remaining solid may appear heavier. These observations are fully consistent with conservation of mass — the ‘missing’ or ‘extra’ mass is simply the gas that left or entered the system. A classic example is the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate: \(CaCO_3(s) \rightarrow CaO(s) + CO_2(g)\). The solid left behind weighs less than the original carbonate because \(CO_2\) gas escapes. The total mass (solid + escaping gas) is unchanged.

Key Fact

Conservation of mass: the total mass of reactants always equals the total mass of products. In open systems, gas escaping the container makes the remaining mass appear less — but the gas is still part of the products. In sealed systems, mass is unchanged.

Some reactions are better described using half-equations that show electron transfer explicitly. These are used for electrolysis (and redox reactions at Higher tier). In electrolysis of molten sodium chloride, at the cathode (negative electrode), sodium ions gain electrons: \(Na^+ + e^- \rightarrow Na\). At the anode (positive electrode), chloride ions lose electrons: \(2Cl^- \rightarrow Cl_2 + 2e^-\). Each half-equation must balance for both atoms and charge. These show clearly that electrolysis involves forced transfer of electrons by an external electrical supply.

Equations are the universal language of chemistry. Whether describing a simple neutralisation (\(HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) \rightarrow NaCl(aq) + H_2O(l)\)), a displacement reaction (\(Zn(s) + CuSO_4(aq) \rightarrow ZnSO_4(aq) + Cu(s)\)), or the combustion of a fuel, the same rules apply: balance atoms, include state symbols, and check that mass is conserved. Learning to write and interpret equations fluently is one of the most transferable skills in chemistry.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When balancing equations in the exam, always write out the atom count on each side — do not try to balance by inspection alone. A common error is changing subscript numbers rather than adding coefficients; this changes the substance and will lose marks. For questions about mass changes in reactions: always ask whether the system is sealed or open. If open, ask whether a gas is produced or absorbed. The correct explanation always refers to atoms being conserved — not created or destroyed.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Chemical equations must be balanced so the number of each type of atom is the same on both sides, reflecting the conservation of mass — atoms are rearranged in reactions but never created or destroyed.
  • State symbols — (s), (l), (g), (aq) — show the physical form of each substance and must be included in full symbol equations.
  • Apparent mass changes in open systems (e.g. gas escaping) are consistent with conservation of mass; in sealed systems the total mass is always unchanged.

practice_questions.text:
Balance the following equation and explain why balancing is necessary:
\(Fe + O_2 \rightarrow Fe_2O_3\)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Gives the correct balanced equation (\(4Fe + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2Fe_2O_3\)); explains that balancing is necessary because the number of atoms of each element must be the same on both sides; links this to conservation of mass (atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed).
Secure: Correct balanced equation and two points of explanation.
Developing: Correct balanced equation but explanation limited.
Emerging: Attempt at balancing with errors; or explanation without correct balanced equation.

practice_questions.text: A student heats 100 g of calcium carbonate in an open crucible and collects 56 g of solid product. The student says: ‘44 g of mass was destroyed in the reaction.’ Evaluate this claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that mass is conserved and is not destroyed; identifies that the reaction is \(CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2\); explains that 44 g of \(CO_2\) was produced as a gas and escaped into the air; that if the gas were collected, total mass of products would be 56 + 44 = 100 g; concludes the student’s claim is incorrect — mass appears to decrease in an open system because a gas product escapes, not because mass is destroyed.
Secure: Correct identification of \(CO_2\) escaping and correct conclusion that mass is conserved.
Developing: States mass is conserved but does not clearly explain the role of the escaping gas.
Emerging: States mass is conserved without explaining the apparent discrepancy.

practice_questions.text: Write a balanced symbol equation with state symbols for the reaction between sodium hydroxide solution and hydrochloric acid solution to form sodium chloride solution and water.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correct balanced equation (\(NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) \rightarrow NaCl(aq) + H_2O(l)\)) with all four state symbols correctly assigned.
Secure: Correct balanced equation; three of four state symbols correct.
Developing: Correct formulae but equation unbalanced or state symbols missing/wrong.
Emerging: One or two correct formulae; no balancing or state symbols.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of chemical equations in communicating what happens during a chemical reaction, including what information they do and do not provide.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains what a balanced symbol equation shows (which substances react and form, in what ratio, physical states via state symbols, conservation of mass); evaluates limitations (equations do not show rate of reaction, activation energy, conditions required, three-dimensional arrangement of atoms, or the mechanism of how bonds break and form); compares word equations (more accessible, less informative) with symbol equations (precise, quantitative, universal language of chemistry); discusses how half-equations extend symbol equations to show electron transfer explicitly; reaches a balanced conclusion about the value of equations as communication tools.
Secure: At least four valid points about what equations do and do not show, with some evaluative language.
Developing: Three points about what equations show; limited evaluation of what is missing.
Emerging: Describes equations briefly without evaluation.
